summary: This informational document collects security considerations for the SHA-0 and SHA-1 hash algorithms. It explains that weaknesses found in these hash functions matter for uses that depend on collisions being hard to find, and discusses what that means for protocols that use them. It is guidance for protocol designers rather than a protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: A hash is a fingerprint for data. This note warns that the fingerprint machines called SHA-0 and SHA-1 have cracks, so two different things can be made to look alike, and builders should be careful.

questions: what are the security issues with sha-1
should i use sha-1 in a new protocol
subtitle: What the published attacks on SHA-0 and SHA-1 mean for protocol designers, and why collision resistance is the weak spot.

tldr.problem: SHA-0 and SHA-1 produce 160-bit message digests, but published attacks show they are weaker than expected, and protocol designers need to know which uses are affected.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC summarizes the known attacks on collision resistance, pre-image resistance, second pre-image resistance and keyed-hash (HMAC) use for each algorithm, then draws conclusions for IETF protocols.
tldr.outcome: SHA-0 should not be used in any IETF protocol, and designers of protocols that use digital signatures should strongly consider a hash with greater collision resistance than SHA-1. HMAC-SHA-1 remains secure.

today: RFC 6194 is an Informational document and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It describes the state of knowledge as of March 2011, and the RFC itself tells designers to review the current state of the art when choosing a hash.

sections.title: Why This Document Exists
sections.content:
SHA-0 (first published in 1993) and SHA-1 (first published in 1996) are message digest algorithms. They take a message of any length and produce a 160-bit "fingerprint" of it. The published attacks against both show that it is not prudent to use either one when collision resistance is required.

The RFC assumes the reader knows RFC 4270, which summarizes how hashes are used in Internet protocols and how attacks on a hash's one-way and collision-free properties do and do not affect those protocols. It also points to NIST guidance on key lengths and algorithm strengths.
sections.plainLanguage: A hash is a short fingerprint for any file or message. This note explains that two of the older fingerprint recipes have cracks in them.

sections.title: SHA-0 Attacks
sections.content:
NIST withdrew SHA-0 in 1996, and the RFC discusses it only for completeness. Any use of SHA-0 is strongly discouraged.

  • Collisions: a 1998 attack finds collisions in 2^61 operations, and a 2006 attack improved this to 2^36 operations. An ideal 160-bit hash would take 2^80, so SHA-0 is far weaker than expected.
  • Pre-images: attacks exist only on reduced versions, for example 49 and 52 of the 80 rounds, with complexities of 2^159 and 2^156. SHA-0 resists these attacks at full strength.
  • HMAC-SHA-0: the best partial key recovery attack needs 2^84 queries and 2^60 SHA-0 computations. Such attacks must be online, because the attacker needs many HMAC values.
sections.plainLanguage: The oldest recipe was found to be so easy to fool that nobody should use it any more.

sections.title: SHA-1 Attacks
sections.content:
The first attack on SHA-1 was published in early 2005 and covered a version reduced to 53 rounds. The next month, an attack showed collisions in the full 80 rounds in 2^69 operations. The RFC says no published result improves on that, although one paper claimed 2^51 hash function calls in an online version that was absent from the published conference paper. Either way, 2^69 is well below the ideal 2^80.

For pre-images, there are no known attacks specific to full-round SHA-1. A general result for narrow-pipe hash functions puts a second pre-image of a 60-byte message at 2^106 computations. The best reduced-round pre-image attack reaches 48 of 80 rounds at complexity 2^159. The RFC warns that reduced-round results show how strong an algorithm is against one attack, not how close it is to being broken.

For keyed use, there is no indication that attacks on SHA-1 extend to HMAC-SHA-1. NIST recommended that SHA-1 not be used for generating digital signatures after December 31, 2010, and not by U.S. federal agencies for protecting sensitive but unclassified information after December 31, 2013.
sections.plainLanguage: The newer recipe also has a crack, but finding it takes a huge amount of work. It is still safe for some jobs, like locking a message with a secret key.

sections.title: Conclusions for Protocol Designers
sections.content:
SHA-1 gives less collision resistance than expected, and that matters for some, but not all, uses of digital signatures. Designers of IETF protocols that use digital signatures should strongly consider supporting a hash with greater collision resistance. SHA-0 should continue to not be used in any IETF protocol.

The RFC does not tell designers to ban SHA-1 outright. Nearly all IETF protocols that use signatures assume existing public key infrastructures, and SHA-1 is still used in signatures nearly everywhere, so strictly prohibiting it is called unwise. Protocols that allow SHA-1 signatures as an option should consider referencing this document in their security considerations.

Two further notes: SHA-1 with randomized hashing (as in NIST SP 800-107) is an option, though it makes signatures larger and means protocols must carry extra material. And HMAC-SHA-1 remains secure and is the preferred keyed-hash algorithm for IETF protocol design. At publication, SHA-256 was the most commonly specified alternative.
sections.plainLanguage: The advice is to switch to a stronger fingerprint where it matters, but not to panic about every old use of the older one.
